name: Brooklyn Community Board 1
about: Brooklyn Community District 1 encompasses Greenpoint and Williamsburg. Covering 4.7 square miles and home to more than 200,000 residents, it sits on the borough's northern edge, where the East River, Newtown Creek, and the Queens line shape the district.

Greenpoint and Williamsburg give the district a mix of waterfront industry, older rowhouse blocks, large apartment development, nightlife, manufacturing, public housing, and ongoing redevelopment along the waterfront and near transit.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 10
about: Brooklyn Community District 10 encompasses Bay Ridge, Dyker Heights, and Fort Hamilton. Covering 4.6 square miles and home to more than 120,000 residents, it covers the southwest corner of the borough, facing the Narrows and Lower New York Bay.

Bay Ridge, Dyker Heights, and Fort Hamilton give the district a mix of waterfront, low-rise residential blocks, apartment corridors, immigrant small businesses, and military history, connected to the rest of the city through transit and local commerce.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 11
about: Brooklyn Community District 11 encompasses Bath Beach, Gravesend, Mapleton, and Bensonhurst. Covering 4.7 square miles and home to more than 180,000 residents, it is a dense southwest Brooklyn district built around residential blocks, commercial avenues, schools, houses of worship, and immigrant communities.

The district is not defined by a single center. It works through a network of corridors, transit lines, and local institutions that serve a large population in a relatively low-rise built environment.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 12
about: Brooklyn Community District 12 encompasses Borough Park, Kensington, Ocean Parkway, and Midwood. Covering 3.6 square miles and home to more than 190,000 residents, it is one of the borough's densest residential districts.

Borough Park, Kensington, Ocean Parkway, and Midwood include apartment buildings, rowhouses, religious institutions, schools, and commercial streets that serve large families and tightly organized communities, in one of the borough's densest residential settings.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 13
about: Brooklyn Community District 13 encompasses Coney Island, Brighton Beach, Bensonhurst, Gravesend, and Sea Gate. Covering 3.3 square miles and home to more than 100,000 residents, it is a waterfront district at the southern edge of the borough.

Coney Island and Brighton Beach bring beaches, amusement areas, high-rise housing, public housing, immigrant commercial corridors, and major seasonal activity into the same district. It is also shaped by coastal risk, transit dependence, aging infrastructure, and the public role of the waterfront.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 14
about: Brooklyn Community District 14 encompasses Flatbush, Midwood, Kensington, and Ocean Parkway. Covering 3.9 square miles and home to more than 160,000 residents, it covers central Brooklyn neighborhoods with strong residential density, subway access, and major commercial corridors.
Flatbush, Midwood, Kensington, and Ocean Parkway include apartment buildings, rowhouses, institutions, schools, and houses of worship serving many overlapping communities.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 15
about: Brooklyn Community District 15 encompasses Sheepshead Bay, Manhattan Beach, Kings Bay, Gerritsen Beach, Kings Highway, East Gravesend, Madison, Homecrest, and Plum Beach. Covering 6.7 square miles and home to more than 160,000 residents, it covers a large part of southeast Brooklyn near the Atlantic Ocean.

Its neighborhoods range from waterfront communities and bungalow blocks to apartment corridors and commercial strips. Sheepshead Bay, Manhattan Beach, Gerritsen Beach, Homecrest, and the Kings Highway area give the district a mix of coastal issues, transportation needs, housing questions, and neighborhood institutions.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 16
about: Brooklyn Community District 16 encompasses Brownsville, Ocean Hill, and part of Bedford-Stuyvesant. Covering 1.9 square miles and home to roughly 85,000 residents, it is centered on Brownsville and Ocean Hill, with part of Bedford-Stuyvesant included in the district.
It has a large public housing presence, residential blocks, schools, parks, churches, and transit corridors.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 17
about: Brooklyn Community District 17 encompasses East Flatbush, Remsen Village, Farragut, Rugby, Erasmus, and Ditmas Village. Covering 3.1 square miles and home to more than 150,000 residents, it covers a large residential section of central and eastern Brooklyn.

East Flatbush, Remsen Village, Farragut, Rugby, Erasmus, and Ditmas Village include rowhouses, apartment buildings, medical institutions, schools, and commercial corridors. The district is large enough to contain several neighborhood identities, but its shared issues are familiar: housing stability, transportation, street safety, public services, and local economic activity.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 18
about: Brooklyn Community District 18 encompasses Canarsie, Bergen Beach, Mill Basin, Flatlands, Marine Park, Georgetown, and Mill Island. Covering 8.8 square miles and home to more than 190,000 residents, it is the borough's largest community district by land area.

It includes Canarsie, Bergen Beach, Mill Basin, Flatlands, Marine Park, Georgetown, and Mill Island, with a built form that ranges from attached houses and garden apartments to waterfront blocks and major parkland.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 2
about: Brooklyn Community District 2 encompasses Boerum Hill, Brooklyn Heights, Clinton Hill, Downtown Brooklyn, DUMBO, Fulton Ferry, Fort Greene, Brooklyn Navy Yard, and Vinegar Hill. Covering 2.8 square miles and home to about 100,000 residents, it is one of the borough's main civic and institutional centers.

It includes Downtown Brooklyn, the courts, major transit hubs, historic residential neighborhoods, and the Brooklyn Navy Yard. The district has a compact geography but a large role in how Brooklyn works, with office towers, public institutions, historic districts, NYCHA campuses, schools, and waterfront redevelopment all sitting close together.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 3
about: Brooklyn Community District 3 encompasses Bedford-Stuyvesant, Stuyvesant Heights, and Ocean Hill. Covering 2.9 square miles and home to more than 150,000 residents, it centers on Bedford-Stuyvesant and Ocean Hill, two neighborhoods with deep civic, cultural, and political histories.
The district is primarily residential, with blocks of brownstones, small apartment buildings, churches, schools, and commercial corridors that carry much of the neighborhood's daily life.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 4
about: Brooklyn Community District 4 encompasses Bushwick. Covering 2 square miles and home to more than 110,000 residents, it is a compact, dense, transit-connected district built around residential blocks, industrial spaces, elevated train corridors, and commercial streets.
Its built environment includes residential blocks, industrial spaces, elevated train corridors, and commercial streets, with many older industrial buildings adapted to new uses.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 5

reps.rep: State Senator Joseph P. Addabbo Jr.

about: Brooklyn Community District 5 encompasses East New York, Cypress Hills, Highland Park, City Line, New Lots, Spring Creek, and Starrett City. Covering 5.6 square miles and home to more than 180,000 residents, it sits on the borough's eastern edge, with Queens to the north and east and Gateway National Recreation Area to the south.

The district includes rowhouse blocks, public housing campuses, large apartment complexes, industrial areas, suburban-style retail, and major open spaces. It is one of Brooklyn's largest districts by population and geography.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 6
about: Brooklyn Community District 6 encompasses Carroll Gardens, Cobble Hill, Columbia Waterfront, Gowanus, Park Slope, Red Hook. Covering 3.1 square miles and home to more than 100,000 residents, it runs from the East River and Upper New York Bay inland toward Prospect Park.

The district combines historic brownstone neighborhoods, active industrial areas, public housing, maritime uses, commercial corridors, and the Gowanus Canal. It is residential in much of its daily life, but the waterfront, Red Hook, and Gowanus give it a land use mix that is broader than a simple brownstone district.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 7
about: Brooklyn Community District 7 encompasses Sunset Park and Windsor Terrace. Covering 4.9 square miles and home to more than 150,000 residents, it stretches from the Gowanus Bay waterfront through Sunset Park and into Windsor Terrace.

The district includes one of the city's most important working waterfronts, a large industrial base, immigrant commercial corridors, rowhouse neighborhoods, and hillside residential blocks near the park.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 8
about: Brooklyn Community District 8 encompasses Crown Heights, Prospect Heights, and Weeksville. Covering 3 square miles and home to roughly 96,000 residents, it sits between Atlantic Avenue and Eastern Parkway.

It has rowhouses, apartment buildings, cultural institutions, historic districts, churches, schools, and major transit corridors. The district's built form changes quickly from block to block, but the central questions are consistent: housing, preservation, commercial corridors, and how growth meets existing communities.

name: Brooklyn Community Board 9
about: Brooklyn Community District 9 encompasses Crown Heights, Prospect Lefferts Gardens, and Wingate. Covering 2.9 square miles and home to more than 100,000 residents, it links central Brooklyn to the eastern side of Prospect Park and the neighborhoods south of Eastern Parkway.
Crown Heights, Prospect Lefferts Gardens, and Wingate give the district a mix of apartment buildings, rowhouses, medical institutions, parkside blocks, and busy commercial streets.

name: Bronx Community Board 1
about: The Bronx Community District 1 encompasses Melrose, Mott Haven, Port Morris, and The Hub. Covering 2.77 square miles and home to roughly 91,000 residents, it sits in the South Bronx at the borough's southern gateway.

Melrose, Mott Haven, Port Morris, and The Hub include industrial areas, public housing, new residential development, major commercial activity, and transit connections to Manhattan and the rest of the Bronx.

name: Bronx Community Board 10
about: The Bronx Community District 10 encompasses City Island, Co-op City, Locust Point, Pelham Bay, Throggs Neck, and Westchester Square. Covering 6.47 square miles and home to more than 120,000 residents, it covers the northeast Bronx and includes some of the borough's most distinct waterfront and lower-density neighborhoods.

City Island, Co-op City, Pelham Bay, Throggs Neck, Locust Point, and Westchester Square create a district with coastal communities, large-scale housing, commercial corridors, parks, and maritime edges.

name: Bronx Community Board 11
about: The Bronx Community District 11 encompasses Allerton, Bronxdale, Indian Village, Laconia, Morris Park, Pelham Gardens, Pelham Parkway, and Van Nest. Covering 3.6 square miles and home to more than 110,000 residents, it covers a residential section of the East Bronx.
It includes apartment buildings, one- and two-family homes, commercial streets, medical institutions, and major roadways, with a largely neighborhood-based built environment.

name: Bronx Community Board 12
about: The Bronx Community District 12 encompasses Baychester, Eastchester, Edenwald, Fish Bay, Olinville, Wakefield, Williamsbridge, and Woodlawn. Covering 5.62 square miles and home to more than 150,000 residents, it covers the borough's northern edge.

Baychester, Eastchester, Edenwald, Wakefield, Williamsbridge, Woodlawn, Olinville, and Fish Bay give the district a mix of apartment buildings, one- and two-family homes, rail connections, parks, and neighborhood commercial streets.

name: Bronx Community Board 2
about: The Bronx Community District 2 encompasses Hunts Point and Longwood. Covering 2.14 square miles and home to roughly 52,000 residents, it includes one of the city's most important food distribution and industrial areas alongside residential blocks, schools, parks, and waterfront infrastructure.
It includes one of the city's most important food distribution and industrial areas alongside residential blocks, schools, parks, and waterfront infrastructure.

name: Bronx Community Board 3
about: The Bronx Community District 3 encompasses Claremont, Crotona Park East, and Morrisania. Covering 1.57 square miles and home to roughly 80,000 residents, it covers a compact section of the South Bronx.
The district includes apartment buildings, public housing, schools, commercial corridors, and important park space. It is a residential district with a long civic history.

name: Bronx Community Board 4
about: The Bronx Community District 4 encompasses Concourse, Concourse Village, and Highbridge. Covering 2.04 square miles and home to more than 140,000 residents, it sits in the west-central Bronx near Yankee Stadium and the Grand Concourse.

The district sits near Yankee Stadium and the Grand Concourse, with dense apartment buildings, public housing, parks, institutions, and heavy transit use. It is one of the borough's most urban community districts.

name: Bronx Community Board 5
about: The Bronx Community District 5 encompasses Fordham, Morris Heights, Mount Hope, University Heights, and Fordham Plaza. Covering 1.37 square miles and home to more than 120,000 residents, it is small in land area and large in population.
The district's apartment corridors, schools, shopping areas, transit hubs, and institutions sit within a small geography that holds a large population.

name: Bronx Community Board 6
about: The Bronx Community District 6 encompasses Bathgate, Belmont, East Tremont, and West Farms. Covering 1.55 square miles and home to roughly 83,000 residents, it sits in the central Bronx near the Bronx Zoo.

The district contains residential blocks, commercial corridors, schools, parks, and the Bronx Zoo area nearby. Belmont gives it a well-known retail and food identity, but the larger district is also shaped by housing needs, transit access, public health, and the daily work of neighborhood institutions.

name: Bronx Community Board 7
about: The Bronx Community District 7 encompasses Bedford Park, Jerome Park, Kingsbridge, Norwood, University Heights, and Fordham. Covering 1.87 square miles and home to more than 130,000 residents, it covers dense neighborhoods of the northwest Bronx.
It includes apartment buildings, colleges, parks, major roads, and transit corridors, functioning as both a residential area and a borough crossroads.

name: Bronx Community Board 8

reps.rep: Council Member Carmen De La Rosa
Assembly Member Manny De Los Santos

about: The Bronx Community District 8 encompasses Fieldston, Kingsbridge, Kingsbridge Heights, Marble Hill, Riverdale, Spuyten Duyvil, and Van Cortlandt Village. Covering 3.41 square miles and home to more than 100,000 residents, it covers the northwest corner of the borough.
It has hills, parks, apartment towers, lower-density residential areas, institutions, and major transportation links, giving it a different feel from much of the Bronx.

name: Bronx Community Board 9
about: The Bronx Community District 9 encompasses Bronx River, Bruckner, Castle Hill, Clason Point, Harding Park, Parkchester, Soundview, and Unionport. Covering 4.79 square miles and home to more than 170,000 residents, it covers a large section of the East Bronx.

Soundview, Parkchester, Castle Hill, Clason Point, Harding Park, Unionport, Bruckner, and Bronx River give the district a mix of large housing complexes, waterfront communities, highways, commercial corridors, and open space.

name: Manhattan Community Board 1
about: Manhattan Community District 1 encompasses TriBeCa, Financial District, Civic Center, Battery Park City, South Street Seaport, part of Chinatown, Battery Park, City Hall Park, Governors Island, Ellis Island, and Liberty Island. Covering 1.5 square miles and home to roughly 64,000 residents, it covers Lower Manhattan, where government, finance, tourism, residential growth, and waterfront infrastructure overlap.

The district includes Tribeca, the Financial District, Civic Center, Battery Park City, the South Street Seaport, part of Chinatown, and several harbor islands. It is small in land area but citywide in importance, with daily issues that range from schools and housing to security, resiliency, transportation, and public space.

name: Manhattan Community Board 10
about: Manhattan Community District 10 encompasses Central Harlem. Covering 1.4 square miles and home to more than 110,000 residents, it contains dense residential blocks, public housing, brownstones, commercial corridors, parks, houses of worship, and major civic institutions.
It contains dense residential blocks, public housing, brownstones, commercial corridors, parks, houses of worship, and major civic institutions, with a deep cultural and political history.

name: Manhattan Community Board 11
about: Manhattan Community District 11 encompasses East Harlem (El Barrio), Randall's Island, and Wards Island. Covering 1.5 square miles and home to more than 120,000 residents, it covers upper Manhattan east of Fifth Avenue, along with Randall's and Wards Islands in the East River.
The district includes public housing, apartment buildings, cultural institutions, hospitals, parks, industrial edges, and major transportation infrastructure.
office: 1664 Park Avenue, Ground Floor, Manhattan, NY 10035

name: Manhattan Community Board 12

reps.rep: Council Member Carmen De La Rosa
Assembly Member Manny De Los Santos

about: Manhattan Community District 12 encompasses Inwood, Washington Heights, and Hudson Heights. Covering 2.9 square miles and home to more than 210,000 residents, it covers the northern end of Manhattan.

The district has large apartment buildings, steep topography, parks, hospitals, schools, commercial corridors, and major transit connections. It is one of Manhattan's most residential community districts.
office: 1112 St Nicholas Avenue, 6th Floor, Manhattan, NY 10032

name: Manhattan Community Board 2
about: Manhattan Community District 2 encompasses Greenwich Village, West Village, South Village, NoHo, SoHo, Hudson Square, Little Italy, and part of Chinatown. Covering 1.4 square miles and home to roughly 90,000 residents, it covers some of the city's most intensely used lower Manhattan neighborhoods.

Greenwich Village, the West Village, South Village, NoHo, SoHo, Hudson Square, Little Italy, and part of Chinatown include historic districts, universities, nightlife, retail corridors, apartment buildings, and heavily used streets.

name: Manhattan Community Board 3
about: Manhattan Community District 3 encompasses Lower East Side, East Village, Alphabet City, Chinatown, and Two Bridges. Covering 1.7 square miles and home to more than 160,000 residents, it sits on the east side of Lower Manhattan, along the East River.
The district has tenements, public housing, nightlife corridors, immigrant institutions, waterfront blocks, and several large development sites.

name: Manhattan Community Board 4
about: Manhattan Community District 4 encompasses Hell's Kitchen and Chelsea. Covering 2.1 square miles and home to more than 100,000 residents, it covers Hell's Kitchen and Chelsea on the west side of Midtown.
The district includes dense residential blocks, major cultural institutions, Hudson River waterfront parks, rail and bus infrastructure, office development, hotels, and nightlife.

name: Manhattan Community Board 5
about: Manhattan Community District 5 encompasses Midtown, Times Square, Herald Square, Midtown South, Flatiron District, part of Murray Hill, part of Chelsea, part of Gramercy, and Union Square. Covering 1.6 square miles and home to roughly 51,000 residents, it is the city's central business district in community-board form.

Midtown, Times Square, Herald Square, Midtown South, the Flatiron District, Union Square, and parts of Chelsea, Murray Hill, and Gramercy place offices, hotels, retail, transit, landmarks, parks, and residential buildings in close contact, with very different daytime, nighttime, and visitor populations.

name: Manhattan Community Board 6
about: Manhattan Community District 6 encompasses part of Murray Hill, Sutton Place, Beekman Place, Turtle Bay, Tudor City, part of Gramercy, Kips Bay, Peter Cooper Village, Stuyvesant Park, and Stuyvesant Town. Covering 1.5 square miles and home to more than 150,000 residents, it covers the east side of Midtown and the blocks running south toward Gramercy and Kips Bay.
It includes major hospitals, the United Nations, apartment towers, older residential blocks, and heavily traveled avenues.

name: Manhattan Community Board 7
about: Manhattan Community District 7 encompasses Upper West Side, Manhattan Valley, and Lincoln Square. Covering 1.9 square miles and home to more than 210,000 residents, it covers the Upper West Side between Central Park and Riverside Park.

The district includes apartment buildings, brownstones, schools, cultural institutions, parks, and major commercial corridors between Central Park and Riverside Park. It is dense, organized, and institution-rich.

name: Manhattan Community Board 8
about: Manhattan Community District 8 encompasses Yorkville, Upper East Side, Lenox Hill, Roosevelt Island, Mill Rock, and Carnegie Hill. Covering 2.5 square miles and home to more than 220,000 residents, it covers the Upper East Side and Roosevelt Island.

It is a district of apartment towers, historic blocks, hospitals, museums, schools, parks, and East River waterfront infrastructure, combining some of the city's highest-density residential areas with major institutions.

name: Manhattan Community Board 9
about: Manhattan Community District 9 encompasses Hamilton Heights, Manhattanville, Morningside Heights, and Columbia University. Covering 1.5 square miles and home to more than 110,000 residents, it covers upper Manhattan between the Hudson River and Harlem.

The district sits between the Hudson River, Harlem, and the institutions of upper Manhattan. It has apartment buildings, public housing, campuses, churches, commercial corridors, and waterfront infrastructure.

name: Queens Community Board 1
about: Queens Community District 1 encompasses Astoria, Ditmars, Long Island City, Queensbridge, Ravenswood, Rikers Island, Steinway, and Woodside. Covering 6.2 square miles and home to more than 170,000 residents, it covers northwest Queens along the East River.

Astoria, Ditmars, Long Island City, Queensbridge, Ravenswood, Steinway, Woodside, and Rikers Island give the district a mix of waterfront industry, large public housing campuses, older residential blocks, new high-rise development, nightlife, and major transportation infrastructure. It is one of the clearest examples of Queens as both a residential borough and a regional employment and infrastructure hub.

name: Queens Community Board 10

reps.rep: State Senator Joseph P. Addabbo Jr.

about: Queens Community District 10 encompasses Howard Beach, South Ozone Park, and Ozone Park. Covering 6.8 square miles and home to more than 120,000 residents, it sits in southern Queens near Jamaica Bay and JFK Airport.

The district includes residential neighborhoods, coastal areas, airport-related traffic, commercial corridors, and major highways. Its geography makes flooding, transportation, infrastructure, public safety, and quality of life constant concerns, especially where local streets carry regional traffic.

name: Queens Community Board 11
about: Queens Community District 11 encompasses Bayside, Douglaston, Little Neck, and Auburndale. Covering 10 square miles and home to more than 110,000 residents, it covers the northeast corner of Queens.
It is largely residential, with lower-density housing, commercial strips, schools, parks, and waterfront edges.

name: Queens Community Board 12
about: Queens Community District 12 encompasses Jamaica, South Jamaica, Hollis, and St. Albans. Covering 9.6 square miles and home to more than 250,000 residents, it is one of the city's largest community districts by population.

Jamaica, South Jamaica, Hollis, and St. Albans include major transit hubs, commercial corridors, residential blocks, institutions, public housing, and large civic assets. The district is a center for southeast Queens.

name: Queens Community Board 13
about: Queens Community District 13 encompasses Laurelton, Cambria Heights, Queens Village, and Glen Oaks. Covering 12.6 square miles and home to more than 190,000 residents, it covers a wide stretch of eastern Queens along the Nassau County line.
It has a lower-density residential pattern than much of the city, with one- and two-family homes, commercial strips, parks, and major roads, spread across a large geographic area.

name: Queens Community Board 14
about: Queens Community District 14 encompasses The Rockaways and Broad Channel. Covering 22 square miles and home to more than 110,000 residents, it covers the Rockaway Peninsula and Broad Channel.
It is a coastal district with beaches, public housing, bungalow communities, apartment buildings, commercial corridors, wetlands, and limited transportation connections to the rest of the city.

name: Queens Community Board 2
about: Queens Community District 2 encompasses Hunters Point, Long Island City, Maspeth, Sunnyside, and Woodside. Covering 5 square miles and home to more than 130,000 residents, it sits between the East River and Newtown Creek in western Queens.
The district contains some of Queens' largest redevelopment areas, active industrial space, rail infrastructure, residential neighborhoods, and busy commercial corridors.

name: Queens Community Board 3
about: Queens Community District 3 encompasses Jackson Heights, East Elmhurst, and North Corona. Covering 2.8 square miles and home to more than 180,000 residents, it sits in northern Queens north of Roosevelt Avenue.
It is one of the city's most diverse and densely used residential districts, with apartment buildings, small homes, immigrant commercial corridors, schools, and heavy transit use.

name: Queens Community Board 4
about: Queens Community District 4 encompasses Elmhurst and Corona. Covering 2.3 square miles and home to more than 160,000 residents, it covers Elmhurst and Corona.

The district is dense and multilingual, built around apartment buildings, small homes, commercial corridors, schools, hospitals, and transit, where the city's immigration story is visible in everyday life.

name: Queens Community Board 5

reps.rep: State Senator Joseph P. Addabbo Jr.

about: Queens Community District 5 encompasses Maspeth, Middle Village, Ridgewood, and Glendale. Covering 7.3 square miles and home to more than 170,000 residents, it sits on the western edge of Queens along the Brooklyn line.

It includes rowhouse neighborhoods, lower-density residential areas, cemeteries, industrial space, rail corridors, and commercial streets. The district often feels less like one center and more like several neighborhoods sharing infrastructure, truck routes, schools, parks, and local business corridors.

name: Queens Community Board 6

reps.rep: State Senator Joseph P. Addabbo Jr.

about: Queens Community District 6 encompasses Rego Park and Forest Hills. Covering 2 square miles and home to more than 110,000 residents, it covers Forest Hills and Rego Park.
The district is compact, residential, and transit-oriented, with apartment buildings, co-ops, single-family homes, commercial corridors, and major roadways.

name: Queens Community Board 7
about: Queens Community District 7 encompasses Flushing, Whitestone, and College Point. Covering 12 square miles and home to more than 250,000 residents, it covers a large part of northeast Queens along the East River and Long Island Sound.

The district ranges from one of the city's busiest commercial and transit centers to waterfront industrial areas and lower-density residential neighborhoods. Its size and variety make it a district where immigration, jobs, congestion, waterfront access, schools, and infrastructure all matter at once.
office: 30-50 Whitestone Ep Sr W, Suite 205, Queens, NY 11354

name: Queens Community Board 8

reps.rep: State Senator Joseph P. Addabbo Jr.

about: Queens Community District 8 encompasses Fresh Meadows, Kew Gardens Hills, and Jamaica Hills. Covering 4.8 square miles and home to more than 150,000 residents, it covers central Queens.
It is primarily residential, with apartment buildings, co-ops, one- and two-family homes, schools, institutions, and major roadways.

name: Queens Community Board 9

reps.rep: State Senator Joseph P. Addabbo Jr.

about: Queens Community District 9 encompasses Woodhaven, Richmond Hill, Ozone Park, and Kew Gardens. Covering 3.1 square miles and home to more than 140,000 residents, it sits in central-southern Queens between Forest Park and the Brooklyn line.

The district includes commercial avenues, residential blocks, transit corridors, parks, and institutions that connect central and southern Queens, with a built environment that shifts from apartments to attached houses to older commercial strips.

name: Staten Island Community Board 1
about: Staten Island Community District 1 encompasses the North Shore neighborhoods, including St. George, Tompkinsville, Stapleton, New Brighton, West Brighton, Port Richmond, Mariners Harbor, Clifton, Rosebank, Silver Lake, Grymes Hill, Westerleigh, and many others. Covering 13.5 square miles and home to more than 170,000 residents, it covers the North Shore, the borough's historic gateway to the harbor and to Manhattan.

The district includes St. George, Tompkinsville, Stapleton, Port Richmond, Mariners Harbor, Clifton, Rosebank, and many other neighborhoods. It has ferry access, waterfront industry, public housing, older commercial corridors, hills, institutions, and some of the borough's densest residential areas.
office: 1 Edgewater Street, Room 217, Staten Island, NY 10305

name: Staten Island Community Board 2
about: Staten Island Community District 2 encompasses the Mid-Island neighborhoods, including New Dorp, Midland Beach, Dongan Hills, New Springville, Grasmere, South Beach, Travis, Todt Hill, Oakwood, Bulls Head, Grant City, Old Town, and many others. Covering 21.3 square miles and home to more than 130,000 residents, it covers the Mid-Island, a large district of residential neighborhoods, commercial centers, parks, wetlands, and major roadways.

New Dorp, Midland Beach, Dongan Hills, New Springville, Grasmere, South Beach, Travis, Todt Hill, and other neighborhoods give it a wide range of built environments across residential areas, commercial centers, parks, wetlands, and major roadways.
office: 900 South Avenue, Suite 28, Staten Island, NY 10314

name: Staten Island Community Board 3
about: Staten Island Community District 3 encompasses Annadale, Arden Heights, Bay Terrace, Charleston, Eltingville, Great Kills, Greenridge, Huguenot, Pleasant Plains, Prince's Bay, Richmond Valley, Rossville, Tottenville, and Woodrow. Covering 21.5 square miles and home to more than 160,000 residents, it covers the borough's South Shore along Raritan Bay and the Atlantic.
The district is predominantly residential, closely tied to coastal geography, wetlands, parks, and local commercial centers.
office: 1243 Woodrow Road, 2nd Floor, Staten Island, NY 10309
